lessons_data.title: Retirement Accounts for Traders: IRAs, Roth IRAs and the Solo 401(k)

content.heading: Retirement Accounts for Traders: IRAs, Roth IRAs and the Solo 401(k)
content.body:
Why the account matters more than the trade

Everything in lessons 1 to 9 applies to a taxable account. Inside an individual retirement account the questions those lessons answer mostly disappear. A traditional IRA is exempt from tax under section 408(e)(1); a Roth IRA under section 408A is treated the same way. Trades inside the account are not reported on Form 8949, there is no short-term versus long-term distinction, no wash-sale adjustment within the account, no $3,000 loss limit and no estimated tax on gains as they occur. Tax arrives, if at all, when money comes out. From a traditional IRA a distribution is ordinary income (plus a 10% additional tax before age 59½ unless an exception applies, Pub. 590-B). From a Roth IRA a qualified distribution, one made after the 5-year period that begins with the first year a Roth contribution was made and on or after age 59½, disability or death, is not taxable at all (Pub. 590-B, What Are Qualified Distributions?).

That is why active trading in a Roth IRA is uniquely efficient: a strategy whose gains are all short-term and would be taxed at up to 37% plus 3.8% in a taxable account compounds without tax drag and can be withdrawn tax-free. The price is that losses inside the account are worth nothing for tax purposes either, the contribution limits are small, and money cannot come out early without cost.

Getting money in

Contributions require compensation. Publication 590-A defines compensation as what you earn from working, wages, salaries, tips, professional fees and net earnings from self-employment, and lists what it does not include, starting with earnings and profits from property. Trading gains are profits from property, and IRS Topic No. 429 says gains of a trader are not subject to self-employment tax, so they are not self-employment earnings either. A full-time trader with no wages and no other business has no compensation and cannot contribute to an IRA at all, even with a profitable year. A spouse with compensation can fund a spousal IRA on a joint return.

The annual limit is set by section 219(b)(5). Notice 2024-80 fixes it at $7,000 for 2025 with a $1,000 additional amount at age 50 or older; Notice 2025-67 raises it to $7,500 for 2026 with an $1,100 catch-up. Roth IRA contributions phase out with modified AGI under section 408A(c)(3): for 2025 between $150,000 and $165,000 for single filers and between $236,000 and $246,000 for joint filers; for 2026 between $153,000 and $168,000 and between $242,000 and $252,000 (Notice 2025-67 and IRS news release IR-2025-111).

The solo 401(k) and why most traders cannot use it

A one-participant 401(k) lets a business owner with no employees contribute twice: as employee, elective deferrals up to $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026 (section 402(g), Notices 2024-80 and 2025-67), plus catch-up of $7,500 (2025) or $8,000 (2026) at 50 or older and $11,250 at ages 60 to 63; and as employer, a profit-sharing contribution. The total, excluding catch-up, cannot exceed the section 415(c) limit of $70,000 for 2025 or $72,000 for 2026. The IRS page on one-participant 401(k) plans states that for a self-employed person compensation means earned income: net earnings from self-employment after deducting half the self-employment tax and the contributions themselves, computed with Publication 560's worksheets. A plan with $250,000 or more in assets at year end files Form 5500-EZ.

For a trader the conclusion follows from Topic 429: trading gains, with or without a section 475(f) election, are not net earnings from self-employment, so they cannot support a solo 401(k) contribution. Traders who have one fund it from other self-employment income, such as consulting, or through an entity structure that pays them compensation; both are outside this course and need a professional, because the plan rules, the reasonableness of compensation and the costs all have to be checked.

Prohibited transactions

Section 4975 and Publication 590-B define a prohibited transaction as any improper use of the IRA by you, your beneficiary or a disqualified person (your fiduciary and your spouse, ancestors, lineal descendants and their spouses). Publication 590-B's examples include borrowing money from the IRA, selling property to it, using it as security for a loan and buying property for personal use with IRA funds. The consequence under section 408(e)(2)(A) is severe: the account ceases to be an IRA as of the first day of the year in which the transaction occurred, and Publication 590-B treats all its assets as distributed to you at fair market value on that day, taxable and possibly subject to the 10% additional tax. Pledging an IRA as collateral for a personal margin loan is the trader's version of this mistake.

UBTI and margin

An IRA is exempt but pays tax on unrelated business taxable income. Section 512(b)(5) excludes gains from the sale of property, so ordinary trading gains in an IRA are not UBTI. Section 512(b)(4) overrides that exclusion for debt-financed property as defined in section 514: income and gain from property bought with acquisition indebtedness, which Publication 598 describes, is included in proportion to the debt. A margin loan used to buy securities inside an IRA is the standard way an IRA acquires such debt. Publication 590-B requires the IRA to file Form 990-T when it has $1,000 or more of gross unrelated business income, by April 15 for a calendar-year IRA, and the trustee may file on its behalf. Many IRA custodians offer limited margin, which settles trades without borrowing; whether a given account borrows is a question for the custodian's documents.

The IRA wash-sale trap

Lesson 3 showed that Publication 550 lists a purchase of substantially identical stock in your IRA or Roth IRA as triggering a wash sale on a loss in your taxable account, and that the basis adjustment does not carry into the IRA. The loss is permanently lost. Automatic dividend reinvestment in an IRA holding the same fund you just harvested in a taxable account is the common way this happens.

Worked example

Trade. You bought 40 TSLA on 2025-03-10 at the Yahoo Finance daily close of $222.15, cost $8,886.00, and sold them on 2025-05-27 at the close of $362.89, proceeds $14,515.60. Gain $5,629.60, held 78 days.

In a taxable account, single filer in the 24% bracket: short-term gain taxed at ordinary rates, $5,629.60 × 0.24 = $1,351.10 of 2025 federal tax, plus 3.8% NIIT ($213.92) if MAGI exceeds $200,000. In a traditional IRA: no 2025 tax; the $14,515.60 is taxed as ordinary income whenever it is withdrawn. In a Roth IRA: no 2025 tax and no tax on a later qualified distribution. Over a year of such trades the difference is the whole short-term tax bill.

Contribution check. You are single, under 50, with wages and 2025 modified AGI of $158,000. Roth contribution limit from Publication 590-A Worksheet 2-2: line 3, $158,000 − $150,000 = $8,000; line 5, $8,000 ÷ $15,000 = 0.533; line 7, $7,000 × 0.533 = $3,731.00; line 8, $7,000 − $3,731.00 = $3,269.00, rounded up to the next multiple of $10 = $3,270. Your 2025 Roth IRA contribution limit is $3,270, and the deadline for a 2025 contribution is the April 15, 2026 due date of the return. For 2026 the same MAGI gives ($158,000 − $153,000) ÷ $15,000 = 0.333; $7,500 × 0.333 = $2,497.50; $7,500 − $2,497.50 = $5,002.50, rounded up to $5,010.

lessons_data.title: Crypto and Forex: Digital Assets as Property, Form 1099-DA and Section 988

content.heading: Crypto and Forex: Digital Assets as Property, Form 1099-DA and Section 988
content.body:
Crypto is property

IRS Notice 2014-21, Q&A-1, says virtual currency is treated as property and that general tax principles applicable to property transactions apply. Publication 550 restates the rule for all digital assets, defined as a digital representation of value recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger: they are property, the holding-period rules of lesson 1 apply, and the guidance list includes Notice 2023-34, Rev. Rul. 2019-24, Rev. Rul. 2023-14 and Rev. Proc. 2024-28. For an individual holding crypto as an investment, a disposal produces capital gain or loss: short-term if held one year or less, long-term if more, taxed exactly as stock gains are.

The property framing has consequences that surprise newcomers. Notice 2014-21, Q&A-6, says exchanging virtual currency for other property produces gain or loss, so trading one token for another is a taxable disposal of the first token at its fair market value in dollars, even though no dollars were involved. Spending crypto on goods is a disposal. Paying a network fee in crypto is a disposal of the coins used. Receiving crypto as payment, as a mining or staking reward, or in an airdrop is ordinary income at fair market value when received (Rev. Rul. 2023-14 for staking), and that value becomes the coins' basis. The IRS digital assets page sends such income to Schedule 1 and capital disposals to Form 8949.

Every Form 1040 also asks whether, at any time during the year, you received digital assets as a reward, award or payment, or sold, exchanged or otherwise disposed of a digital asset. Merely buying with dollars and holding is a No; any disposal is a Yes.

Basis by wallet and the wash-sale question

Treasury Regulation 1.1012-1(j), applicable from 2025, requires basis to be identified for digital assets held in each wallet or account separately: specific identification is allowed if made in your records (unhosted wallets) or communicated to the broker (custodial accounts), and otherwise first-in, first-out applies wallet by wallet. Rev. Proc. 2024-28 gave a safe harbour under section 1012(c)(1) for allocating unused basis to wallets and accounts as of January 1, 2025, based on your records of that basis. A single universal FIFO pool across every exchange, the method many people used before 2025, is no longer the default.

IRC section 1091 applies to stock or securities. The guidance cited here treats digital assets as property, not securities, and does not apply section 1091 to them, which is why a crypto loss can generally be realised and the coin repurchased immediately. There is one exception visible in the forms: the 2026 Form 1099-DA instructions require brokers to report wash-sale losses on tokenized securities, digital assets that are themselves stock or securities, in box 1i. Whether a particular token is a security is a legal question this course does not answer.

Form 1099-DA

Section 6045, as amended by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, extended broker reporting to digital assets. The IRS digital assets page says brokers must report gross proceeds on Form 1099-DA for transactions on or after January 1, 2025. The 2026 Form 1099-DA instructions add mandatory basis reporting for digital assets that are covered securities, defined as assets acquired after 2025 for cash or other property in an account where the broker provides custodial services and held there until sold. In practice your 2025 Forms 1099-DA show proceeds without basis, and you must supply basis from your own records. Assets transferred into an exchange from elsewhere are noncovered and stay that way. The Form 8949 instructions created boxes G, H and I (short-term) and J, K and L (long-term) for digital asset transactions and say not to use boxes A to F for them; a 2025 short-term sale reported on a 1099-DA without basis goes in Part I with box H checked.

Forex: section 988 by default

Currency trading has its own section. IRC section 988 applies to foreign currency transactions including acquiring nonfunctional currency, and to forward contracts, futures contracts and options on currencies. Section 988(a)(1)(A) treats foreign currency gain or loss on a section 988 transaction as ordinary income or loss. For an individual trading spot currency with a retail dealer, the default is therefore ordinary treatment: gains taxed at ordinary rates, losses fully deductible against other income without the $3,000 capital loss cap. Section 988(e) excludes personal transactions, such as currency bought for travel, and section 988(e)(2) ignores gains of $200 or less on personal disposals of foreign currency.

Two routes lead out of ordinary treatment. Section 988(a)(1)(B) lets you elect capital treatment for a forward contract, futures contract or option that is a capital asset in your hands and not part of a straddle, but only if you make the election and identify the transaction before the close of the day you enter into it. Whether a rolling spot contract at a retail forex dealer qualifies as a forward contract for this election is not addressed in the sources cited here; confirm it with a CPA before relying on it. Second, section 988(c)(1)(D) removes from section 988 any regulated futures contract or nonequity option that would be marked to market under section 1256. A currency futures contract on the CME is therefore a section 1256 contract by default and gets the 60/40 treatment of lesson 5, unless you elect out of that exception under section 988(c)(1)(D)(ii) by the first day of the tax year. An interbank forward that qualifies as a foreign currency contract under section 1256(g)(2) is also a section 1256 contract.

Worked example

Crypto. You bought 0.5 BTC on a custodial exchange on 2025-04-07 at the Yahoo Finance BTC-USD daily close of $79,235.34, cost $39,617.67, and sold it on 2025-10-06 at the close of $124,752.53, proceeds $62,376.27. Gain = $62,376.27 − $39,617.67 = $22,758.60. Holding period from 2025-04-08 to 2025-10-06 is under a year, so short-term. Tax at a 24% marginal rate: $22,758.60 × 0.24 = $5,462.06. Had you held until 2026-04-08 or later, the gain would have been long-term at 15% in the same bracket, before any price change.

Reporting. Your 2025 Form 1099-DA shows gross proceeds of $62,376.27 and no basis, because the coins were acquired before 2026 and are noncovered. On Form 8949, Part I, box H: (a) 0.5 BTC; (b) 04/07/2025; (c) 10/06/2025; (d) $62,376.27; (e) $39,617.67 from your records; (h) $22,758.60. Answer Yes to the digital asset question on Form 1040.

Forex. A trader with $150,000 of wages lost $12,000 trading spot EUR/USD with a retail dealer in 2025 and made no section 988(a)(1)(B) election. The loss is ordinary under section 988(a)(1)(A) and reduces taxable income by the full $12,000, worth $12,000 × 0.24 = $2,880 in the 24% bracket. Had the same $12,000 been a capital loss with no capital gains to absorb it, section 1211(b) would have allowed $3,000, worth $720, with $9,000 carried forward. Had it been a $12,000 gain, it would be taxed at 24% ($2,880) under section 988, but at the 18.6% blended rate ($2,232) if it had come from CME euro futures under section 1256.

lessons_data.title: Record-Keeping: Form 8949, Schedule D, the 1099-B and Working With a CPA

content.heading: Record-Keeping: Form 8949, Schedule D, the 1099-B and Working With a CPA
content.body:
How the forms fit together

A trader's capital transactions travel through three layers. Brokers report each sale to you and the IRS on Form 1099-B (securities) or Form 1099-DA (digital assets), and report section 1256 contracts in aggregate in 1099-B boxes 8 to 11. You transcribe and correct those sales on Form 8949, one row per sale or one summary row per category with an attached statement. Form 8949 totals, Form 6781 for section 1256 contracts, capital gain distributions and any carryover from last year meet on Schedule D, which produces the net figure on Form 1040 line 7 and feeds the capital gain tax worksheet. A trader with a section 475(f) election instead reports trading-business securities on Form 4797 Part II line 10, with an attached statement listing each transaction and separately identifying positions marked at year end (Form 4797 instructions).

The Form 8949 instructions explain the purpose: it lets you and the IRS reconcile the amounts reported on information returns with the amounts on your return. That is the right way to think about it. The IRS matches your Schedule D to the 1099-Bs it received; your job is to report the broker's numbers and then show, in columns (f) and (g), exactly where and why your numbers differ.

The six boxes and the two exceptions

Part I of Form 8949 is short-term and Part II long-term, using the holding-period rule of lesson 1. Each part is filed separately for each box. Box A (Part I) or D (Part II): reported on a 1099-B showing basis was reported to the IRS. Box B or E: reported on a 1099-B without basis reported to the IRS. Box C or F: no 1099-B at all. Digital assets use G, H, I and J, K, L instead (lesson 11). Check one box per page.

Exception 1 lets you skip Form 8949 for sales on a 1099-B that shows basis reported to the IRS, shows no adjustment in box 1f (accrued market discount) or box 1g (wash sale loss disallowed), and does not have the Ordinary box checked; report their totals directly on Schedule D line 1a (short-term) or line 8a (long-term). Exception 2 lets you report all sales on an attached statement in the same format, typically the broker's own realised gain/loss report, and enter only the totals on Form 8949 with the broker's name and "see attached statement" in column (a). Don't write "available upon request" in place of the detail.

Reconciling the 1099-B

Read the 1099-B before you trust it. Check four things. First, that every sale you made appears, including option expirations and assignments, which brokers sometimes show in a separate section. Second, the basis on noncovered lots, which brokers are not required to report: stock acquired before 2011 and anything transferred in without basis information arrives as box B or E with a blank or wrong basis, and you supply it. Third, box 1g, which the broker fills only for wash sales within the same account and CUSIP (1099-B instructions); wash sales across accounts, brokers, your spouse or your IRA are yours to find. Fourth, section 1256 aggregates in box 11, which go to Form 6781, not Form 8949.

Form 8949 column (f) codes record each correction: W for a wash-sale loss you cannot deduct (positive amount in column (g)); B when the basis on the 1099-B is incorrect (reported basis stays in column (e), correction in column (g) if basis was reported to the IRS); O for other adjustments; and several more for special cases. The Worksheet for Basis Adjustments in Column (g) computes a code B adjustment as reported basis minus correct basis.

Worked example

This is lesson 3's wash sale, with the repurchase made at a second broker so neither firm sees it.

Broker A, 2025 Form 1099-B, box 12 checked (basis reported): 100 SPY acquired 2025-02-19, sold 2025-04-04; box 1d proceeds $50,528.00; box 1e basis $61,293.00; box 1g $0.00. Broker B, 2025 Form 1099-B, box 12 checked: 100 SPY acquired 2025-04-24, sold 2025-12-01; box 1d $68,027.00; box 1e $54,669.00; box 1g $0.00. All prices are Yahoo Finance daily closes for SPY.

Your own wash-sale check finds that the 2025-04-24 purchase at Broker B falls inside the window 2025-03-05 to 2025-05-04 around the 2025-04-04 loss sale at Broker A. Section 1091 disallows the $10,765.00 loss and adds it to the replacement's basis: $54,669.00 + $10,765.00 = $65,434.00.

Form 8949, Part I, box A, row 1 (Broker A sale): (a) 100 sh SPY; (b) 02/19/2025; (c) 04/04/2025; (d) $50,528.00; (e) $61,293.00; (f) W; (g) $10,765.00; (h) = $50,528.00 − $61,293.00 + $10,765.00 = $0.00.

Row 2 (Broker B sale): (a) 100 sh SPY; (b) 04/24/2025, the trade date of the replacement purchase as column (b) instructs; (c) 12/01/2025; (d) $68,027.00; (e) $54,669.00, the basis Broker B reported; (f) B; (g) basis worksheet: reported $54,669.00 minus correct $65,434.00 = −$10,765.00; (h) = $68,027.00 − $54,669.00 − $10,765.00 = $2,593.00. The tacked holding period, from 2025-02-20, is still under a year, so Part I is correct either way.

Totals carried to Schedule D line 1b: (d) $118,555.00; (e) $115,962.00; (g) $10,765.00 − $10,765.00 = $0.00; (h) $2,593.00. The IRS sees both 1099-B amounts in columns (d) and (e) exactly as reported, and the codes explain the difference. Had you filed the two 1099-Bs as reported, your 2025 return would have shown a $10,765.00 loss and a $13,358.00 gain, the same $2,593.00 net in this case because both legs closed in 2025; had the replacement still been open on December 31, the unreported wash sale would have overstated your 2025 loss by $10,765.00.

Table

Record Keep until Source
Return and supporting records, general case 3 years after filing (a return filed early is treated as filed on the due date) IRC 6501(a); IRS, How long should I keep records
If income omitted exceeds 25% of gross income shown 6 years after filing IRC 6501(e)(1)(A); same
Claim for a worthless-securities or bad-debt loss 7 years IRS, How long should I keep records
No return filed, or a fraudulent return Indefinitely IRC 6501(c); same
Purchase confirmations and basis records for a position Until the limitation period expires for the year you dispose of it IRS, How long should I keep records
Worked example: the 2025-02-19 SPY confirmation At least until April 15, 2029 (3 years after the April 15, 2026 due date of the 2025 return) Same

Working with a CPA

Bring documents, not summaries. A CPA or enrolled agent preparing a trader's return needs: every Form 1099-B, 1099-DA, 1099-DIV and 1099-INT, including corrected forms, which brokers often issue in March; the consolidated statements and realised gain/loss detail behind them; your own lot records for noncovered positions and for crypto by wallet; a list of every account you and your spouse hold, including IRAs, for the cross-account wash-sale check; the prior year's return with Schedule D and the Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet; the dated section 475(f) election statement and Form 3115 if you have elected; Form 1040-ES payment confirmations; and the trading-expense records from lesson 8 if you claim trader status. Ask how they will test trader status, how they handle same-index fund replacements, and whether they file Form 8949 by transaction or by attached statement. A preparer can only defend what you can document, and every position in this course, from specific identification to trader status, rests on records made at the time.

Sources

  • Instructions for Form 8949 (boxes A to L; Exceptions 1 and 2; codes W and B; Worksheet for Basis Adjustments): https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i8949
  • Instructions for Schedule D (Form 1040), 2025: https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1040sd
  • Instructions for Form 1099-B (box 1g; boxes 8 to 11): https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099b
  • IRS, How long should I keep records?: https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/how-long-should-i-keep-records

quiz.q: Under Exception 1 in the Form 8949 instructions, you may skip Form 8949 and report totals directly on Schedule D line 1a or 8a when:
opts: The broker reported basis to the IRS and the 1099-B shows no adjustments in box 1f or 1g, and the Ordinary box is not checked
You have fewer than 100 trades
All trades were profitable
You used a CPA
quiz.explain: Exception 1 covers transactions (other than collectibles) on a 1099-B showing basis reported to the IRS, with no adjustment in box 1f or 1g and the Ordinary box in box 2 unchecked. Anything with an adjustment must go on Form 8949.

quiz.q: Your broker reported the basis of replacement shares as $54,669 to the IRS, but the correct basis after a cross-account wash sale is $65,434. On Form 8949 Part I, box A, you enter:
opts: $65,434 in column (e) and nothing in column (g)
$54,669 in column (e), code B in column (f), and −$10,765 in column (g)
$54,669 in column (e) and code W
Nothing; the broker's figure is final
quiz.explain: The Form 8949 instructions for code B: when the basis was reported to the IRS, enter the reported basis in column (e) even though it is incorrect, and correct it in column (g) using the Worksheet for Basis Adjustments (reported basis minus correct basis).

quiz.q: Generally, how long must you keep records supporting an item on a return, if no special situation applies?
opts: 1 year
10 years
Until the period of limitations for that return runs out, generally 3 years after filing
Forever
quiz.explain: IRS, How long should I keep records: keep records until the period of limitations expires, generally 3 years (IRC section 6501(a)); 6 years if you omit more than 25% of gross income; 7 years for a worthless securities or bad debt loss; indefinitely for no return or a fraudulent return.

quiz.q: Records showing what you paid for shares should be kept:
opts: Until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the shares
3 years from purchase
Until the next 1099-B arrives
Only if the shares are noncovered
quiz.explain: The IRS records page: keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property, because you need them to figure gain or loss.

quiz.q: For a trader with a section 475(f) election, trading-business securities sales are reported on:
opts: Form 8949 with code W
Schedule D line 1a
Form 6781
Form 4797 Part II line 10, with an attached statement
quiz.explain: The Form 4797 instructions: report on line 10 all gains and losses from securities held in connection with the trading business, including year-end marks, with a statement in the same format showing each transaction, and enter 'Trader—see attached' in column (a).

lessons_data.title: Capstone: A Twelve-Trade Tax Year, From Trade List to Schedule D

content.heading: Capstone: A Twelve-Trade Tax Year, From Trade List to Schedule D
content.body:
The exercise

You are preparing the 2025 federal return of a single filer. The facts: wages $120,000 on Form W-2; no other income; standard deduction $15,750 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.01, as amended for 2025); no capital loss carryover from 2024; no section 475 election in effect. All stock and ETF trades were made in one taxable brokerage account, all shares were covered securities with basis reported to the IRS, and every sale used specific identification confirmed by the broker in writing, so the lots sold are exactly those listed. The futures were traded at a separate futures broker. Prices are Yahoo Finance daily closes on the dates shown. MES, the Micro E-mini S&P 500 future, has a $5 multiplier per index point (a CME contract specification, not an IRS figure).

Answer five tasks. One: classify each trade as short-term, long-term or section 1256 and compute its gain or loss. Two: identify the wash sale, the disallowed amount, the adjusted basis of the replacement shares and their holding period. Three: complete the Form 8949 summary lines, Form 6781 lines 1, 7, 8 and 9, and Schedule D lines 1b, 4, 7, 8a or 8b, 11, 15 and 16. Four: compute the 2025 federal income tax under scenario A (trades as listed) and scenario B (trade 1's NVDA sold on 2025-07-02 at $157.25 instead of 2025-06-30), and state whether the net investment income tax applies. Five: explain what would change if a securities-only section 475(f) election had been in effect for 2025, and when it would have had to be made.

The trade list

# Ticker Qty Bought Buy price Sold Sell price
1 NVDA 100 2024-07-01 $124.30 2025-06-30 $157.99
2 SPY 50 2025-02-19 $612.93 2025-04-04 $505.28
3 SPY 50 2025-04-24 $546.69 2025-12-01 $680.27
4 TSLA 40 2025-03-10 $222.15 2025-05-27 $362.89
5 QQQ 30 2025-01-06 $524.54 2025-04-07 $423.69
6 AAPL 60 2025-06-20 $201.00 2025-12-15 $274.11
7 IWM 100 2025-04-08 $174.82 2025-12-19 $250.79
8 TSLA 20 2025-09-15 $410.04 2025-12-22 $488.73
9 NVDA 50 2025-01-24 $142.62 2025-02-24 $130.28
10 QQQ 30 2025-06-02 $523.21 2025-11-03 $632.08
11 AAPL 50 2024-08-01 $218.36 2025-10-17 $252.29
12 MES (2 contracts, long) 2 2025-11-20 6,557.50 open at 2025-12-31 6,892.50 (2025-12-31 close)

Worked example

This is the model answer. Work the exercise before reading it.

Task 1, classification. Gains are proceeds minus cost, quantity times price. Trade 1: $15,799.00 − $12,430.00 = $3,369.00; held from 2024-07-02 to 2025-06-30, under a year, short-term. Trade 2: $25,264.00 − $30,646.50 = −$5,382.50, short-term. Trade 3: $34,013.50 − $27,334.50 = $6,679.00 before adjustment, short-term. Trade 4: $14,515.60 − $8,886.00 = $5,629.60. Trade 5: $12,710.70 − $15,736.20 = −$3,025.50. Trade 6: $16,446.60 − $12,060.00 = $4,386.60. Trade 7: $25,079.00 − $17,482.00 = $7,597.00. Trade 8: $9,774.60 − $8,200.80 = $1,573.80. Trade 9: $6,514.00 − $7,131.00 = −$617.00. Trade 10: $18,962.40 − $15,696.30 = $3,266.10. Trades 4 to 10 are all short-term. Trade 11: $12,614.50 − $10,918.00 = $1,696.50, held from 2024-08-02 to 2025-10-17, long-term. Trade 12 is a regulated futures contract, a section 1256 contract (lesson 5), marked at the 2025-12-31 close: (6,892.50 − 6,557.50) × $5 × 2 = $3,350.00.

Task 2, the wash sale. Trade 2 sold SPY at a loss on 2025-04-04; trade 3 bought 50 SPY on 2025-04-24, 20 days later and inside the window 2025-03-05 to 2025-05-04. Section 1091(a) disallows all $5,382.50, because the same number of shares was repurchased. Section 1091(d): trade 3's basis becomes $27,334.50 + $5,382.50 = $32,717.00, and its holding period includes trade 2's, so it runs from 2025-02-20; trade 3 is still short-term at 2025-12-01. Trade 3's reported gain is $34,013.50 − $32,717.00 = $1,296.50. Because both trades were in one account with one CUSIP, the broker reports $5,382.50 in 1099-B box 1g for trade 2 and the adjusted $32,717.00 in box 1e for trade 3. No other loss is affected: trade 5's QQQ loss on 2025-04-07 has no QQQ purchase between 2025-03-08 and 2025-05-07 (trade 10 is 2025-06-02), and trade 9's NVDA loss on 2025-02-24 has no NVDA purchase between 2025-01-25 and 2025-03-26. Holding trade 1's older NVDA lot through that window does not matter: section 1091 looks for acquisitions.

Task 3, the forms, scenario A. Form 8949 Part I, box A, all ten short-term sales: column (d) $179,079.40; (e) $160,985.80; (g) $5,382.50 (trade 2, code W); (h) $23,476.10. Equivalent and acceptable: trade 2 alone on Form 8949 and the other nine on Schedule D line 1a under Exception 1; the line 7 result is identical. Part II, box D, trade 11: (d) $12,614.50; (e) $10,918.00; (h) $1,696.50, which qualifies for Exception 1 and may go directly on Schedule D line 8a. Form 6781: line 1, $3,350.00 (1099-B box 11 from the futures broker); line 7, $3,350.00; line 8 (40%), $1,340.00; line 9 (60%), $2,010.00. Schedule D: line 1b, $23,476.10; line 4, $1,340.00; line 7, $24,816.10; line 8a or 8b, $1,696.50; line 11, $2,010.00; line 15, $3,706.50; line 16, $28,522.60.

Task 4, the tax. Rates from Rev. Proc. 2024-40, Table 3 and section 2.03. Taxable income before trading: $120,000 − $15,750 = $104,250. Scenario A: ordinary taxable income = $104,250 + $24,816.10 = $129,066.10; tax = $17,651 + 24% × ($129,066.10 − $103,350) = $17,651 + $6,171.86 = $23,822.86. Net capital gain $3,706.50 sits above that, inside the 15% band (which runs to $533,400): $3,706.50 × 15% = $555.98. Total 2025 income tax $24,378.84. Without the trades it would be $17,651 + 24% × $900 = $17,867.00, so the trading year cost $6,511.84.

Scenario B: trade 1 sells on 2025-07-02 for $15,725.00, a $3,295.00 gain, long-term because the holding period now exceeds one year. Part I loses the NVDA row: (d) $163,280.40; (e) $148,555.80; (g) $5,382.50; (h) $20,107.10. Part II gains it: (d) $28,339.50; (e) $23,348.00; (h) $4,991.50. Schedule D line 7 = $21,447.10; line 15 = $7,001.50. Ordinary taxable income $125,697.10; tax = $17,651 + 24% × $22,347.10 = $23,014.30. Capital gain tax: $7,001.50 × 15% = $1,050.23. Total $24,064.53, which is $314.31 less than scenario A on a gain that was $74.00 smaller. A sale on 2025-07-01 would still have been short-term.

NIIT: modified AGI is $120,000 + $28,522.60 = $148,522.60 in scenario A and $148,448.60 in B, below the $200,000 threshold of IRC section 1411(b), so no NIIT.

Task 5, a section 475(f) election. To be effective for 2025 the statement had to be filed by April 15, 2025 with the 2024 return or extension request (Rev. Proc. 99-17 section 5.03; Topic 429), and the taxpayer must actually qualify as a trader, which twelve trades in a year almost certainly do not support. Assuming both: the eleven securities trades go on Form 4797 Part II line 10 as ordinary income, not Form 8949. Section 1091 no longer applies to them, so trade 2's $5,382.50 loss is allowed and trade 3's gain is $6,679.00 on its unadjusted basis; the net is unchanged at $25,172.60 because both legs closed in 2025. No securities were open at year end, so there is no mark. Trade 12 stays under section 1256 at 60/40, because a commodities election under section 475(f)(2) is separate. Ordinary taxable income = $104,250 + $25,172.60 + $1,340.00 = $130,762.60; tax = $17,651 + 24% × $27,412.60 = $24,230.02; plus $2,010.00 × 15% = $301.50; total $24,531.52. That is $152.68 more than scenario A: trade 11's long-term gain lost its 15% rate. Trading expenses would move to Schedule C (lesson 8). The election helps a losing year or a year of heavy cross-period wash sales. It does not help this one.

quiz.q: Trade 1 bought NVDA on 2024-07-01. Which sale date is the earliest that makes the gain long-term?
quiz.explain: Counting begins the day after purchase, 2024-07-02. A sale on 2025-07-01 is exactly one year, which is not more than one year (IRC section 1222). 2025-07-02 is the first long-term date.

quiz.q: Trade 2's $5,382.50 SPY loss is disallowed because:
opts: SPY is an ETF
Trade 3 bought 50 SPY on 2025-04-24, within 30 days after the 2025-04-04 loss sale
The loss exceeded $3,000
SPY is a section 1256 contract
quiz.explain: IRC section 1091(a): the purchase of substantially identical shares within 30 days after the loss sale disallows the loss, and section 1091(d) adds it to the replacement shares' basis.

quiz.q: Trade 3's adjusted basis after the wash-sale adjustment is:
How much of trade 12's MES gain is long-term on Form 6781 line 9?
opts: $0, because it was held 41 days
quiz.explain: IRC section 1256(a)(3): 60% of $3,350.00, the gain marked at the 2025-12-31 close, is long-term, $2,010.00; 40%, $1,340.00, is short-term.

quiz.q: Under a securities-only section 475(f) election the capstone's 2025 tax rises by $152.68. Why?
opts: The wash-sale loss is disallowed twice
Trade 11's $1,696.50 long-term AAPL gain becomes ordinary and loses the 9-point gap between 24% and 15%
The MES gain becomes ordinary
The NIIT applies
quiz.explain: With the election the wash sale is ignored but the total securities result is the same $25,172.60, because both SPY legs closed in 2025. The only change is character: $1,696.50 × (24% − 15%) = $152.685, or $152.68 with the arithmetic carried through.
